Title: Structured Critical Literature Review Generation via Hierarchical
Contradiction-Aware Synthesis---

Problem
Current automated literature review systems (LLM-based or
retrieval-augmented) produce fluent but shallow summaries — they list findings
paper-by-paper, avoid conflicting results, and fail to organize knowledge into
the canonical sub-topics, debates, and open questions a human reviewer would
surface. No existing system explicitly models contradictions across papers or
generates a structured review with sections like "consensus findings,"
"conflicting evidence," and "methodological gaps."

Hypothesis
A hierarchical, contradiction-aware pipeline that (1) retrieves and
clusters papers by sub-topic, (2) extracts claim-level triples (method, finding,
direction of effect), and (3) explicitly identifies and resolves or flags
contradictions, will produce literature reviews that are rated by domain experts
as more organized, more critical, and more useful than retrieval-augmented
baselines that only summarize per-paper or per-topic.

Method
Stage1 — Hierarchical topic structuring. Given a query (e.g.
"chain-of-thought reasoning"), query a paper corpus (e.g. S2ORC / Semantic
Scholar) and cluster retrieved abstracts using a hierarchical embedding +
LLM-labeling pipeline (HDBSCAN on SBERT embeddings, then GPT-4o-mini assigns
canonical section headings).

Stage2 — Claim extraction and contradiction detection. For each paper, extract
structured claim triples (entity, predicate, direction/sign) via a fine-tuned
DeBERTa-v3 or prompted LLM. Within each sub-topic cluster, compare claim triples
for directional mismatches (e.g. "CoT improves accuracy on GSM8K" vs "CoT does
not improve accuracy on GSM8K"). Flag contradictions with supporting citations
on both sides.

Stage3 — Contradiction-aware synthesis. Generate the review section-by-section
using a controlled generation loop: (a) draft a section from the consensus
claims, (b) conditionally append a "conflicting evidence" sub-section if
contradictions were detected, (c) append an "open questions" sub-section
identifying gaps where evidence is absent or contradictory.

Stage4 — Citation grounding and fact verification. Each generated claim is
back-linked to the original source passage. A lightweight fact-verification step
(NLI-based, e.g. TrueTeacher) verifies whether the generated claim is entailed
by the cited passage. Unverifiable claims are removed or softened.

Dataset / Benchmark- Corpus: Semantic Scholar Open Research Corpus (S2ORC) — ~8M
papers, with full text when available. Restrict to4-5 well-surveyed domains
(e.g., LLM reasoning, protein folding, adversarial robustness, representation
learning, NLP for low-resource languages).

• Gold-standard reviews: For each domain, collect2-3 human-written survey
papers (e.g. from arXiv, JMLR, ACL anthology). Segment into sections as
ground-truth structure.
• Review quality evaluation set: Construct50 query-review pairs per domain,
each with3 expert ratings along organization, coverage, critical depth, and
usefulness (1–5 Likert).

Evaluation Metrics| Dimension | Metric | How measured |

|---|---|---| | Structure | Section overlap (ROUGE-L / Jaccard on section
headings) | Against human survey TOC | | Coverage | Recall of cited papers from
human survey reference list | Macro-averaged per section | | Critical depth |
Contradiction recall — fraction of known conflicting findings surfaced |
Hand-labeled conflict set | | Faithfulness | % of claims entailed by cited
passages | NLI-based verification + human spot-check | | Overall quality |
Expert rating (1–5) on organization, usefulness | Blind rating by3 domain
experts |

Baselines1. Naive RAG — Retrieve top-20 papers, concatenate abstracts, prompt
GPT-4o to write a review.

2 Per-paper summarization — Summarize each paper individually, then concatenate
under LLM-generated headings (Liu et al.,2024-style).
3 Topic-cluster summarization — Cluster papers by topic, summarize cluster,
then synthesize (similar to Scim,2024).
4 Ours w/o contradiction detection — Same pipeline but skip Stage2
contradiction flagging (ablate the core mechanism).

Ablations- A1: Remove hierarchical clustering → flat topic list (tests whether
hierarchy improves organization).

• A2: Remove fact-verification filter (tests whether filtering reduces
hallucination at the cost of coverage).
• A3: Replace GPT-4o claim extraction with fine-tuned DeBERTa-v3 (tests whether
a smaller model suffices).
• A4: Remove contradiction-aware sub-section generation → always write
consensus-only text (tests the value of explicit contradiction flagging vs.
implicit handling).

Expected Failure Modes1. Contradictions are rare or subtle. Most papers in a
well-matured field may agree on fundamentals, leaving little for the
contradiction module to surface. Mitigation: evaluate on at least one rapidly
evolving domain (e.g., LLM reasoning post-2023) where disagreements are common.

2 Claim extraction noise propagates. A false-positive contradiction (two claims
that appear contradictory but differ in experimental setup) degrades the
review. Mitigation: require supporting citations on both sides; add a
confidence threshold for contradiction flagging.
3 Expert raters prefer concise over critical. Human readers may rate a fluent,
uncontroversial summary higher than one that honestly reports messy
disagreements. Mitigation: structure expert evaluation to score critical
depth and usefulness separately from fluency and organization.
4 Structure diversity across human surveys. Two human surveys on the same topic
often use different section taxonomies, making section-overlap metrics noisy.
Mitigation: use macro-averaged ROUGE-L and report variance; also report
expert agreement (Fleiss' κ) on organization.
5 Domain shift. A pipeline tuned on NLP papers may fail for biomedical or
physics literature where citation practices and claim phrasing differ.
Mitigation: hold out one domain for final evaluation only, to measure
generalization.

question: Generate a research proposal on low-resource speech recognition.
answer_a:
Low-Resource Speech Recognition via Decoupled Acoustic-Phonetic Pretraining with
  Targeted Decoder Adaptation## ProblemEnd-to-end automatic speech recognition
 (ASR) for low-resource languages (under10 hours of transcribed speech) suffers
 from a fundamental tension: self-supervised speech encoders (e.g., wav2vec2.0,
    HuBERT) learn rich acoustic representations from unlabeled data, but the
randomly initialized decoder collapses into overfitting on the tiny labeled set
   during fine-tuning. Combined full-model fine-tuning forces the encoder to
 overwrite general-purpose representations to accommodate the decoder's random
  initialization, destroying cross-linguistic transfer. Current methods either
   freeze the encoder entirely (sacrificing language-specific adaptation) or
fine-tune jointly (sacrificing representation generality). The community lacks a
  principled approach that decouples which parameters learn what: the encoder
 should retain its universal acoustic-phonetic knowledge while only the decoder
    and a lightweight adapter should adapt to the target language's phoneme
                             inventory and lexicon.

HypothesisDecoupled training — where a frozen self-supervised encoder feeds a
randomly initialized transformer decoder through a Gated Adapter Module (GAM)
that is the only trained component alongside the decoder — will outperform full
fine-tuning and frozen-encoder baselines on ≤10-hour transcribed benchmarks,
achieving >15% relative word error rate reduction while requiring fewer total
updated parameters. The hypothesis rests on the claim that the encoder's
pretrained representations already contain sufficient phonetic discriminability
for the target language; the bottleneck is the decoder's inability to map those
representations to the target token set without corrupting the encoder.

Method**Stage1: Encoder Selection and Freezing.**Use a multilingual wav2vec2.0
XLSR-53 encoder (pretrained on53 languages, ~600k hours of unlabeled speech).
Freeze all transformer layers. Only the input feature encoder (CNN frontend) and
position embeddings remain trainable to handle language-specific acoustic shifts
(vowel quality, prosody). This is a minimal concession — fewer than2% of total
parameters.

**Stage2: Gated Adapter Module (GAM).**Insert a2-layer bottleneck adapter
between the frozen encoder output and the decoder input, with a learned gating
mechanism:


 z = LayerNorm(encoder_output)
 h = GELU(W_down · z) # bottleneck: d_model →64gate = σ(W_gate · z) # scalar
 per time-stepadapter_output = gate · (W_up · h) + (1 − gate) · z```

 The gate lets the model *per-time-step* decide whether to route through the
 adapter or pass through the original representation unchanged. This prevents
 the adapter from distorting encoder representations on frames where they are
 already well-calibrated for the target language. GAM contributes ~1.2M
 parameters.

 **Stage3: Decoder Training.**The decoder is a6-layer transformer
 (character-level CTC decoder with a language-specific output vocabulary
 of200–400 graphemes). Train the decoder + GAM jointly with CTC loss.

 **Stage4: Optional Self-Training Loop.**After convergence, generate
 pseudo-labels on unlabeled target-language data (if available). Select
 high-confidence frames (posterior >0.9) and retrain GAM + decoder on the
 combined set. This is a *single* iteration — no iterative refinement
 (consistent with the single-run, non-evolving constraint).

 ## Dataset / Benchmark| Dataset | Language | Labeled Hours | Unlabeled Hours |
 Domain |
 |---|---|---|---|---|
 | Common Voice (Swahili) | Swahili |8.2 |120 | Crowdsourced read speech |
 | Common Voice (Tamil) | Tamil |6.8 |85 | Crowdsourced read speech |
 | MLS (Kinyarwanda) | Kinyarwanda |4.5 |0 | Audiobook read speech |
 | FLEURS (Farsi) | Farsi |10.0 |0 | Read speech,5 domains |

 Four languages spanning three language families (Niger-Congo, Dravidian,
 Indo-European) with varied phoneme inventories, ensuring results are not
 language-specific. The split also provides two datasets with unlabeled data
 (for self-training) and two without (for isolated low-resource assessment).

 ## Evaluation Metrics| Metric | Primary / Secondary | Rationale |
 |---|---|---|
 | Word Error Rate (WER) | Primary | Standard ASR metric, directly comparable |
 | Character Error Rate (CER) | Secondary | Captures morphologically rich
 language degradation |
 | Parameter update ratio | Diagnostic | (# updated params) / (# total params),
 to verify decoupling claim |
 | Time-to-convergence | Diagnostic | Training steps to reach best WER,
 measuring optimization stability |

 All WER/CER reported with95% confidence intervals from3 random seeds per
 condition. Statistical significance assessed with paired bootstrap resampling
 (p <0.05).

 ## Baselines1. **Full Fine-Tuning (FFT).** Unfrozen XLSR-53 encoder + random
 decoder. Standard approach for low-resource ASR.
 2. **Frozen Encoder (FE).** Entire encoder frozen, train decoder only.
 Represents the current state-of-the-art for extremely low-resource settings.
 3. **Adapter without Gate.** GAM without the per-time-step gating mechanism
 (constant residual). Isolates the contribution of the gating mechanism.
 4. **Full Adapter (no bottleneck).** Adapter with d_model → d_model (no
 bottleneck). Tests whether the bottleneck is necessary or if a full-rank
 adapter achieves the same result with more parameters.

 ## Ablations| Ablation | What changes | What it tests |
 |---|---|---|
 | **No GAM** | Remove adapter entirely; train decoder directly on frozen
 encoder output | Whether any adapter is necessary at all |
 | **No gate** | Remove gating; use standard residual adapter | Contribution of
 per-step gating |
 | **Bottleneck width** | Vary bottleneck dim:16,64,256 | Sensitivity to
 compression; the64-dim choice |
 | **Trainable CNN frontend off** | Freeze the input feature encoder entirely |
 Whether the2% parameter allowance matters |
 | **No self-training** | Skip pseudo-label Stage4 | Contribution of the
 single-round self-training |

 ## Expected Failure Modes1. **Language mismatch in the pretraining corpus.**
 XLSR-53 covers53 languages. If the target language is typologically distant
 from all covered languages (e.g., a tonal language with no tonal-language
 pretraining data), the frozen encoder may lack the relevant phonetic
 discriminability. Expect WER degradation on such languages; the GAM cannot
 invent acoustic distinctions the encoder never learned. Mitigation: select
 languages with varying distance from XLSR-53 coverage; report WER vs.
 phylogenetic distance as a diagnostic.

 2. **GAM gate collapse.** The gating mechanism may converge to a trivial
 solution: gate ≈0 everywhere (bypass adapter entirely, equivalent to frozen
 encoder baseline) or gate ≈1 everywhere (disabling the residual connection,
 making GAM a standard adapter). Monitor gate statistics over training; if
 all-time-step mean gate lies outside [0.2,0.8], training is degenerate.

 3. **Self-training confirmation bias.** The single self-training iteration may
 reinforce decoder errors if the pseudo-label threshold (0.9) is too permissive
 or too strict. Character-level analysis of pseudo-labeled vs. ground-truth
 distribution on a held-out subset will quantify error amplification.

 4. **Catastrophic forgetting through CNN frontend.** Although only the CNN
 frontend is trainable (2% of parameters), aggressive learning rates could
 still shift the feature distribution enough to degrade downstream
 representations. Monitor encoder output norm drift as a diagnostic.

 ## Limitations- The method assumes access to a pretrained multilingual speech
 encoder. Languages with no phylogenetic overlap to any pretraining language
 remain out of scope. The method does not propose new pretraining; it exploits
 existing frozen representations.
 - Character-level CTC decoding imposes a conditional independence assumption
 that degrades on languages with long-range phonological dependencies (e.g.,
 vowel harmony in agglutinative languages). A future iteration would replace
 CTC with a transducer or attention-based decoder, but that would conflate
 representation adaptation with decoding architecture changes.
 - The single-round self-training (Stage4) is deliberately limited to remain
 consistent with the non-evolving design constraint. Multi-round self-training
 or iterative pseudo-label refinement could yield additional gains but is
 excluded by experimental design.
 - Evaluation is limited to read-speech domains (Common Voice, MLS, FLEURS).
 Conversational and noisy-condition generalization is not tested. Performance
 on spontaneous, code-switched, or child speech is unknown.
 - The adapter adds ~1.2M parameters and one forward pass per frame (two linear
 layers + gating). Real-time factor impact is not measured; latency-critical
 deployments would need a separate efficiency analysis.

Research Proposal: Confidence-Gated Iterative Pseudo-Labeling with
Phoneme-Constrained Augmentation for Low-Resource ASRTitle: Semi-Supervised
Self-Training with Audited Pseudo-Labels and Phoneme-Preserving Augmentation for
Under-10-Hour Speech Recognition---

Problem
State-of-the-art ASR systems (e.g., Whisper, wav2vec2.0) degrade
catastrophically when fine-tuned on fewer than10 hours of transcribed speech.
Two failure modes dominate: (1) overfitting to the small labeled set, and (2)
confirmation bias in self-training, where the model reinforces its own errors
through noisy pseudo-labels on unlabeled data. No existing method jointly
addresses label quality and data diversity in the under-10-hour regime on a
single pipeline.

Hypothesis
A self-training loop that audits pseudo-labels through a separate
confidence calibrator (rather than the ASR model's own softmax) and couples them
with phoneme-preserving augmentations (time-stretch, pitch-shift, and speed
perturbation clipped to per-phoneme duration bounds) will outperform standard
pseudo-labeling and unsupervised pre-training when labeled data ≤10 hours. The
key claim: auditing prevents confirmation bias, and phoneme-constrained
augmentation prevents the augmentations from destroying linguistic content that
the small labeled set cannot recover.

Method1. Seed model — Fine-tune a small SSL encoder (wav2vec2.0 Base, ~95M
params) on the labeled set (≤10 h). Use a single linear projection head.

2 Pseudo-labeling loop (3 rounds):

• Decode the unlabeled pool with the current model (CTC greedy decoding).
• Audit each pseudo-label: pass the logits to a separate lightweight confidence
estimator (a2-layer MLP over mean-pooled encoder features, trained on the
seed set's held-out fold) and retain only utterances where estimated
confidence ≥0.9 threshold.
• Combine audited pseudo-labeled utterances with the original labeled set.

3 Phoneme-constrained augmentation — Before each training epoch, apply:

• Time stretching (0.85x–1.15x) with per-phoneme duration floor.
• Pitch shift (±2 semitones).
• Speed perturbation (0.9x–1.1x).
• Constraint: a forced-alignment phoneme recognizer (pretrained multilingual)
verifies that the augmented audio's phoneme sequence matches the original;
discard any augmentation where >20% of phonemes shift.

4 Re-train the SSL encoder + projection head from the seed checkpoint on the
combined (labeled + audited pseudo-labeled + augmented) data. Repeat for3
rounds.

Dataset / Benchmark- Primary: Common Voice (Tamil, Sinhala, Catalan, Kyrgyz —4
languages with2–8 h of validated train data each). Evaluate on each language's
official dev/test splits.

• Secondary (sanity check): FLEURS10-hour subset for2 additional languages
(Swahili, Bengali).

Evaluation Metrics| Metric | Purpose |

|---|---| | Character Error Rate (CER) | Primary metric; report mean ± std over3
seeds. | | Word Error Rate (WER) | Secondary, for languages with space-delimited
orthography. | | Pseudo-label acceptance rate | Diagnostic: % unlabeled
utterances retained per round. | | Oracle accuracy of accepted pseudo-labels |
Diagnostic: if a held-out reference exists for the unlabeled pool, measure what
fraction of accepted labels are correct. |

Report effect sizes with95% bootstrap confidence intervals across seeds.

Baselines| Baseline | Why |

|---|---| | Seed-only (fine-tune on labeled data only, no self-training) | Lower
bound — isolates the value of unlabeled data. | | Standard pseudo-labeling (no
auditing, no augmentation) | Ablates the audit mechanism. | | No-augmentation
self-training (audit + pseudo-label, no phoneme constraint) | Ablates the
augmentation contribution. | | SpecAugment self-training (SpecAugment instead of
phoneme-constrained augmentation) | Compares against a widely-used augmentation
baseline. | | wav2vec2.0 Base fine-tuned on full Common Voice (where available,
e.g., Catalan ~80 h) | Upper bound — what performance looks like with abundant
data. | | Whisper Small zero-shot | Compares against a strong multitask model
that has never seen the target language during adaptation. |

Ablations1. Audit threshold sweep — Vary the confidence threshold
(0.7,0.8,0.9,0.95) on one language to measure the precision-recall trade-off in
pseudo-label acceptance.

2 Augmentation constraint strength — Compare the phoneme-preserving constraint
against an unconstrained version (same augmentations, no phoneme-validity
check).
3 Number of self-training rounds — Compare1,2,3, and5 rounds on one language to
measure when performance plateaus or degrades.
4 Size of labeled seed — Sub-sample to1 h,2 h,5 h on a language with8 h
available, and measure whether the method's advantage grows as labeled data
shrinks.

Expected Failure Modes1. Phoneme-constraint too aggressive — The multilingual
forced-aligner may have poor accuracy on a target language it was not trained
on, causing most augmentations to be discarded. Mitigation: Relax the threshold
to40% phoneme shift tolerance; also measure the discard rate and report it.

2 Confidence estimator is poorly calibrated — On languages far from the seed
set, the auditor may either accept noisy labels (false positive) or reject
correct ones (false negative). Mitigation: Use temperature scaling (Platt

long-range reasoning) saturate earlier than others (e.g., syntactic fluency,

precise structural causes of saturation in small models and design targeted
interventions that reallocate limited capacity to the binding constraints?

Primary hypothesis: The performance ceiling in small models is driven
by capacity-competition between world-knowledge memorization and compositional
reasoning pathways, not by a global lack of parameters. When a small model
saturates, additional training data primarily overfits its already-congested
feedforward memory (FFN layers) while the attention-based compositional routing
remains underutilized.

functions — compressing factual knowledge into a fixed, non-parametric memory
(retrieval augmentation with a small bottleneck) and freeing FFN parameters for
compositional reasoning — will raise the ceiling by10–20% on reasoning-heavy
benchmarks while matching or exceeding baselines on factual recall.

long-range reasoning (5+ hops), and in-context learning. Use influence functions
and representation similarity (CKA between hidden states at different data
scales) to identify which layers/modules saturate first and correlate with which

factual recall while lower attention layers saturate for compositional
reasoning.

Research Proposal: Compositional Grounding for Multi-Step Reasoning in
  Tool-Augmented Language Agents## ProblemLarge language models (LLMs) achieve
  strong performance on isolated reasoning benchmarks (e.g., GSM8K, MATH) but
  degrade sharply when deployed as agents that must interleave reasoning with
     external tool calls. The core challenge is not reasoning capacity but
 compositional grounding: the agent must decide when to rely on a tool, how to
 format its output for the tool, and how to integrate the tool's response back
  into its reasoning trace — all while maintaining coherence across a growing
    action history. Current agent frameworks handle this with brittle prompt
  engineering (ReAct, Reflexion) that breaks under distribution shift, and no
  existing benchmark jointly measures the reasoning–tool–memory triplet under
                      controlled compositional variations.

HypothesisAgents fail on multi-step reasoning-with-tools not because the
underlying LLM lacks reasoning ability, but because the compositional interface
between reasoning and tool-use is undertrained. Specifically, we hypothesize
that a compositional-granularity taxonomy — decomposing tasks by (a) number of
tool-call decision points, (b) depth of tool-output integration (surface-passing
vs. structural reformatting), and (c) recency-dependency of prior tool outputs —
predicts agent failure modes better than aggregate accuracy, and that a
structured training curriculum built on this taxonomy can close the gap without
architectural changes.

MethodWe propose a three-phase methodology:

Phase1 — Taxonomy and Benchmark Construction. Define a3 ×3 ×3 design space:


 Dimension               Levels
 Decision points (D)     1,3,5 tool-call junctures
 Integration depth (I)   Surface (pass tool output verbatim into next prompt),
                         Reformatted (extract key fields and restructure),
                         Aggregated (merge multiple tool outputs before
                         reasoning)
 Recency dependency (R)  Independent (each step depends only on initial state),
                         Chain-1 (depends on immediately prior tool output),
                         Chain-3 (depends on outputs from three steps back)


From this space we sample9 task families (one per D-I-R cell) covering
calculator, retrieval, code-execution, and database-query tools, creating1800
instances (200 per cell,20 held-out per cell for validation).

Phase2 — Failure-Mode Profiling. Run a representative set of current agent
frameworks (ReAct, Reflexion, Plan-and-Solve, Tree-of-Thought with tool calls)
across all1800 instances using GPT-4o and Llama-3-70B. Record per-instance:
final accuracy, step-wise tool-call accuracy, and integration fidelity (whether
the agent correctly used the tool output in the subsequent reasoning step). Map
failures onto the D-I-R cell structure.

Phase3 — Targeted Curriculum Training. Construct a training curriculum ordered
by the failure-rate gradient from Phase2 (easiest cell first). Fine-tune a base
Llama-3-8B on this curriculum with a loss that reweights steps where integration
fidelity is low. Evaluate held-out instances from each cell and compare to
uniform-data fine-tuning and prompt-based baselines.

Dataset / BenchmarkNo existing benchmark covers the D-I-R compositional design
space. We build CompoTool-1800:

 • Tool types: calculator (Python eval-like), knowledge retrieval (Wikipedia
   snippet API), code execution (sandboxed Python exec), database query (SQLite
   over synthetic tables)
 • Task templates: multi-hop arithmetic with calculator calls, fact-verification
   with retrieval + calculator, data-analysis pipelines with SQL + Python,
   mixed-tool planning tasks- Splits:1600 train (sampled uniformly across
   cells),200 validation (20 per cell held out for controlled evaluation)
 • Contamination check: all tool outputs are procedurally generated; no overlap
   with public datasets## Evaluation Metrics1. Primary: Cell-level accuracy
   (average per D-I-R cell) — the main metric that tests whether the taxonomy
   captures failure patterns2. Integration fidelity (per-step): binary indicator
   of whether the agent correctly incorporated tool output into the next
   reasoning step, measured by an automated verifier3. Tool-call precision:
   fraction of tool calls that used the correct tool with the correct
   arguments4. Composite difficulty score: weighted average across D, I, R
   dimensions, used to test monotonicity (accuracy should decrease as composite
   score increases)

 5 Cross-model rank consistency: Spearman correlation between model rankings on
   CompoTool-1800 vs. existing agent benchmarks (AgentBench, ToolBench) to
   validate that our benchmark measures something not already captured##
   Baselines1. ReAct (Yao et al.,2023) — thought–action–observation loop,
   zero-shot2. Reflexion (Shinn et al.,2023) — verbal self-reflection on
   failures3. Plan-and-Solve (Wang et al.,2023) — plan-first then execute4.
   Tree-of-Thought with tool-call leaves (Yao et al.,2024 variant) —
   breadth-first search over reasoning + tool paths5. Direct prompting (no agent
   scaffolding) — single-prompt with interleaved instructions, included to
   measure the ceiling of in-context abilityAll baselines run with GPT-4o and
   Llama-3-70B. The Phase3 fine-tuned model is compared against a uniform-data
   fine-tuned Llama-3-8B (same compute budget) and the base Llama-3-8B with
   ReAct.

Ablations1. No tool-output integration verifier: remove the step-wise fidelity
weighting from the curriculum loss to isolate its contribution2. Random-order
curriculum: shuffle the cell ordering in Phase3 to test whether the
difficulty-gradient ordering is necessary3. Single tool type: restrict training
to only calculator tasks to measure cross-tool generalization4. No fine-tuning:
compare the fine-tuned model to the base model with a hand-crafted prompt
template for each cell (rule-based adaptation of ReAct)

Expected Failure Modes1. Surface integration ceiling: agents that pass tool
outputs verbatim without structural reformatting may hit an accuracy ceiling
around D=3, I=Reformatted — the taxonomy predicts this, and it may be
irreducible with current transformer architectures2. Recency decay: Chain-3
instances will likely show accuracy near random beyond4–5 steps regardless of
model size, consistent with known attention sink and lost-in-the-middle
effects3. Curriculum overfitting: the fine-tuned model may specialize to the
D-I-R cell boundaries and fail on instances that fall between cells (e.g., D=2,
I=Reformatted, R=Chain-2 — an untrained cell)

 4 Verifier noise: the automated integration-fidelity verifier may itself err on
   complex cases (e.g., when a tool output is correct but the agent uses it
   indirectly), introducing label noise into the curriculum loss## Limitations1.
   Tool repertoire is fixed: only four tool types, all with clean input/output
   schemas. Real-world agents interact with dozens of heterogeneous, poorly
   documented APIs. Generalization to open-ended tool sets is untested.
 5 Synthetic instance generation: procedurally generated tasks lack the
   ambiguity of human-generated queries. Performance on CompoTool-1800 may
   overestimate real-world robustness.
 6 No multi-turn user interaction: the benchmark assumes a single user query
   with a linear tool-use trace. Conversational agents that revisit earlier
   steps or take user feedback mid-trajectory are out of scope.
 7 Single-turn fine-tuning: the curriculum training uses offline supervised
   learning on successful trajectories. Online (RL-based) methods such as
   outcome-driven reward modeling may yield different conclusions about the
   taxonomy's utility.

   to70B+ models, which exhibit different error patterns (more false positives
   than false negatives in tool-call decisions). The baseline profiling with
   GPT-4o and Llama-3-70B partially addresses this, but the fine-tuning
   experiment is limited to8B.

Title**"Plan-Trace-Verify: A Controlled Study of Multi-Step Compositional
Reasoning in LLM Agents Under Distractor Conditions"**

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Problem
LLM-based agents today are deployed on tasks that require chaining
multiple reasoning steps (e.g., "book a flight, check the weather at the
destination, then find restaurants within budget"). These agents frequently fail
not because individual steps are hard, but because they lose the thread when
intermediate results contradict expectations or when irrelevant context
(distractors) is injected mid-trajectory.

The core problem: existing benchmarks evaluate reasoning in clean, single-turn
settings (e.g., GSM8K, MATH, HotpotQA), but agentic reasoning involves iterative
plan-trace cycles where earlier outputs become inputs to later steps. We lack a
controlled benchmark that isolates the effect of "distractor injection" —
irrelevant or misleading intermediate observations — on compositional reasoning
accuracy.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Hypothesis
H₁ (Primary): Injecting task-irrelevant but semantically plausible
observations mid-trajectory degrades LLM agent compositional reasoning accuracy
by ≥25% relative to the no-distractor baseline, even when the underlying
reasoning path is unchanged.

H₂ (Mechanism): The degradation is primarily driven by retrieval interference
(the agent attends to distractor tokens in subsequent reasoning steps) rather
than plan corruption (the agent incorrectly revises its plan). This implies that
improving selective attention (e.g., structured memory) will help more than
improving planning ability.

H₃ (Mitigation): A simple Plan-Trace-Verify loop — where the agent explicitly
writes down its plan before execution, traces each step against the plan after
receiving observations, and verifies consistency before proceeding — recovers
≥80% of the performance gap relative to the no-distractor baseline.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Method
### Framework: Plan-Trace-Verify (PTV)

We define three agent strategies to compare:

1 Direct-ReAct (baseline): Standard ReAct-style agent — thinks, acts, observes
in a flat loop with no explicit plan tracking.
2 Plan-then-Execute (ablation control): The agent writes a plan (as pseudocode

re-check consistency after each observation.
3 Plan-Trace-Verify (PTV) (proposed): The agent:

postconditions for each step.

Text-to-SQL via Constrained Decoding with Schema-Aware Prefix Tuning##
   ProblemTranslating natural language questions into executable SQL queries
remains a core challenge in semantic parsing. Despite recent progress with large
language models, two persistent failure modes limit deployment: (1) hallucinated
  table/column names that do not exist in the target schema, and (2) logically
    incorrect but syntactically valid SQL that passes execution checks while
    returning wrong answers. Existing approaches rely on either fine-tuning
encoder-decoder models on large synthetic datasets (expensive, brittle to schema
shift) or prompting closed-source LLMs with schema serialization (inconsistent,
   no guaranteed schema adherence). No current method jointly enforces schema
   validity at the token level while learning a structured alignment between
                     question tokens and database columns.

HypothesisConstraining the decoder's output space to the union of schema tokens
and SQL grammar tokens, combined with a lightweight prefix that encodes
question–column alignment scores, will eliminate schema hallucination and
improve logical correctness on compositional queries. The schema constraint is a
hard filter — the decoder can only emit tokens that appear in the active
database schema or the SQL keyword vocabulary — so hallucination is structurally
impossible. The prefix module learns a soft alignment between question spans and
table/column candidates, providing the decoder with grounded attention without
requiring a separate entity-linking pass.

MethodSchema-Augmented Prefix Network. For a given question (q) and database
schema (S = {T_1, \dots, T_k}) where each table (T_i) has columns ({c_{i1},
\dots, c_{im}}), we compute a question-aware schema representation. Each column
(c_{ij}) is encoded as a concatenation of its name, type, and a sampled cell
value. A bi-affine scorer computes alignment scores between each question token
and each column, producing a schema-grounded prefix vector that is prepended to
the decoder's hidden states at every decoding step.

Constrained Decoding with Schema Masking. At each timestep, the output
vocabulary is masked to the union of:

 • SQL reserved keywords (SELECT, FROM, WHERE, JOIN, GROUP BY, etc.)
 • Table names in (S)
 • Column names in (S)
 • Literal tokens (numbers, strings delimited by quotes)
 • Punctuation and operatorsTokens outside this set receive (-\infty)
   log-probability. This mask is recomputed per example since each database has
   a different schema.

Training Objective. Standard cross-entropy on gold SQL tokens, plus an auxiliary
alignment loss that minimizes the KL divergence between the bi-affine attention
weights and a soft alignment derived from the gold SQL's column references. The
two losses are summed with equal weight.

Dataset / BenchmarkSpider (train/dev split,10k questions /200 databases). We
also evaluate on Spider-Syn (synonym-substituted questions) and Spider-DK
(domain-knowledge questions) to test robustness to lexical variation and
implicit reasoning. For cross-domain generalization, we report on the Spider-CG
split (cross-domain compositional generalization). Execution accuracy on the dev
set is the primary metric.

Evaluation Metrics- Execution Accuracy (EX): percentage of predictions whose
execution output matches the gold output on a held-out SQLite instance. The
primary metric.

 • Exact Set Match (EM): exact SQL string match after normalization (column
   order, alias removal). A secondary metric.
 • Token-Level Schema Adherence (SA): percentage of generated tokens that belong
   to the allowed schema+keyword mask. Should be100% by construction; reported
   as a sanity check.
 • Column Recall: fraction of gold-referenced columns that appear in the
   predicted SQL. Measures grounding completeness.

Baselines- T5-3B + Schema Serialization (standard fine-tuning): schema
serialized as a flat text prefix table_name | column_name : type.

 • T5-3B + Schema Linking + SQL Sketch: a two-stage pipeline with an explicit
   entity linker followed by sketch-based decoding. Represents the strongest
   published pipeline for Spider.
 • Codex (code-davinci-002) few-shot prompting:8 annotated examples in the
   prompt, schema serialized as DDL statements. Zero fine-tuning.
 • PICARD (constrained decoding on T5): token-level validation on top of a
   standard T5 decoder; rejects invalid SQL prefixes. Direct comparison for
   constrained-decoding baselines.

All baselines are run on the same Spider train split and evaluated on the
identical dev set. Three random seeds per method to estimate variance.

Ablations| Ablation | Component removed | Expected effect |

|---|---|---| | No schema mask | Hard constraint on output vocabulary removed;
only prefix network remains | Schema hallucination returns; EX drops5–10 points
| | No prefix network | Bi-affine alignment removed; only schema mask remains |
Column recall drops on complex joins; EX drops2–4 points | | No auxiliary
alignment loss | Only cross-entropy on SQL tokens | Slower convergence; EX1–2
points lower after full training | | No cell-value sampling | Column
representation uses name + type only | Performance degrades on ambiguous columns
with similar names |

Expected Failure Modes- Very large schemas (100+ columns): the masked vocabulary
grows linearly with schema size. At inference, softmax over1000+ tokens may
become tractable but slower. Latency impact should be measured.

 • Value-dependent queries (e.g., "find employees named Smith" where "Smith" is
   a literal, not a column): the schema mask allows quoted strings, but the
   decoder must still learn to produce the correct literal. The prefix network
   does not help with literal prediction.
 • Compositional generalization to unseen join patterns: if the training set has
   no examples of joining two specific tables together, the alignment module has
   no training signal for that column pair. The schema mask alone cannot bridge
   this gap.
 • Domain shift in synonyms (Spider-Syn): the schema mask only allows column
   names as they appear in the DDL, not synonyms. If the question uses "worker"
   and the column is "employee", the prefix alignment score for that column may
   be low, but the mask still forces the decoder to use the correct name. This
   is a feature rather than a bug, but it means the model must learn rigid
   lexical mappings.

LimitationsThe constrained decoding approach guarantees schema validity at the
token level but does not guarantee logical correctness — a query that references
the right columns may still compute the wrong aggregate or miss a join
condition. The mask is also schema-specific and must be recomputed per database,
adding a pre-processing step at inference. The bi-affine prefix network is
trained on gold alignments derived from the SQL, which are noisy: multiple
column references in a long query may align to overlapping question spans.
Finally, the approach does not handle queries that require creating intermediate
views or nested subqueries with aliases in a schema-not-present way; these
remain future work.

Large-Scale Databases## Title
Schema-Aware Decomposition: Robust Text-to-SQL on
Large-Scale Databases via Progressive Pruning and Incremental Construction

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Problem
Current LLM-based Text-to-SQL systems perform competitively on benchmarks
like Spider (medium-scale, ~200 tables across20 databases, ~5 tables per
question). However, they degrade sharply on large-scale schemas (50+
tables,1000+ columns) common in enterprise settings. Two core issues:

1 Context window saturation — the full schema cannot fit in a single prompt,
forcing truncation that may drop relevant tables/columns.
2 Schema linking fragility — lightweight retrievers (embeddings + cosine
similarity) miss indirect matches (e.g., a column named "emp_salary" for a
question about "monthly compensation"), while heavy multi-stage pipelines
(re-ranking, self-consistency) inflate cost and latency.

No existing method jointly addresses both problems with a unified, training-free
decomposition that scales to schema sizes beyond current benchmarks.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Hypothesis
Decomposing the Text-to-SQL task into three sequential stages —
structured schema pruning, sub-query decomposition, and incremental SQL
construction with local verification — will improve execution accuracy on
large-scale schemas by ≥15% over flat prompting approaches, while adding ≤2x
inference cost.

The hypothesis rests on two claims:

• Schema pruning by structure + semantics (not just flat embeddings) reduces
irrelevant context without dropping critical tables.
• Incremental construction catches composition errors (missing JOINs, wrong
nesting) at the sub-query level before final assembly.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Method
A three-stage pipeline, SaDec (Schema-Aware Decomposition):

Stage1: Hybrid Schema Pruning- Structure-aware filter: Extract the subgraph of
tables within2-hop relations of user-specified entities (heuristic: tables whose
primary keys appear in the question text, then their foreign-key neighbors).

• Semantic reranker: Embed each remaining table's DDL +3 sample rows using a
bi-encoder (e.g., BGE-M3). Rerank by cosine similarity against the question
embedding. Keep top-K tables (K =8–12, tunable).
• Output: a pruned schema (DDL + foreign keys) small enough to fit in one LLM
call.

Stage2: Sub-Query Decomposition- Prompt an LLM (e.g., GPT-4o-mini) to split the
question into2–5 sub-questions, each referencing specific tables/columns from
the pruned schema.

• Each sub-question is paired with its expected output columns and JOIN
constraints. This acts as an interpretable intermediate plan.

Stage3: Incremental SQL Construction + Verification- Generate SQL for each
sub-question independently, using the pruned schema.

• Local verifier: Execute each sub-query against the database. If it returns an
error or an empty result set, regenerate with a feedback prompt ("previous
attempt failed because...").
• Assembly pass: Combine sub-queries into the final SQL using a separate LLM
call with the full question, sub-queries, and their verified results as
context.
• Optional final check: Run the assembled SQL; if it errors, fall back to a
single-stage generation on the pruned schema.

No fine-tuning required. All stages use frozen LLMs with few-shot prompts (3
exemplars from similar databases in the training set).

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Dataset / Benchmark
Primary evaluation on BIRD-SQL (2024), specifically its
large-scale subset (databases with ≥30 tables: ~15–20 databases, ~1,500
questions). BIRD contains real databases with dirty values and requires external
knowledge — a harder, more realistic setting than Spider.

For controlled analysis, also evaluate on Spider-Syn (schema synonym variant,
~700 questions) and Spider-Realistic (~500 questions with paraphrased
questions), which stress schema linking.

If results are strong, test a synthetic Spider-XL dataset constructed by
concatenating3–4 Spider databases into a single schema (~60 tables,200+ columns)
with200 cross-database questions written by hand.
